Welcome toAdding Random Numbers

Add N random numbers and rescale the sum: how fast does its density become Gaussian?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: the central limit theorem: the density of a standardised sum of N independent random numbers

About this simulation

On screen
The exact density of z = (UN − Nμ)/(σ√N) as a solid blue curve, with the standard Gaussian density e−z2/2/√(2π) as a dashed curve, on fixed axes: z from −4 to 4 and density from 0 to 1.1. A short vertical bar labelled “largest gap” marks where the two curves are furthest apart.
Controls
The parent chooses uniform on 0 to 1 or exponential e−x; N sets how many independent draws are added, 1 to 30. Changing the parent keeps N.
Measured
The density of UN is the parent sampled on a fine grid and convolved with itself N − 1 times by FFT, with no random numbers. Nμ and σ√N are the mean and standard deviation of UN; the largest gap is the maximum of |solid − dashed| over the grid points with |z| ≤ 4.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two uniform numbers

Choose the uniform parent and set N = 1, so that the solid curve is a flat box. Before moving to N = 2, predict the shape of the density of the sum of two uniform numbers.

2 · Three uniform numbers

Keep the uniform parent at N = 2. Before setting N = 3, predict how the solid curve compares with the dashed Gaussian.

3 · Why the width stays put

Keep the uniform parent and set N = 4, where the readouts show that U4 has mean 2 and standard deviation 0.577. Before raising N to 16, predict what happens to the width of the solid curve along the z axis.

4 · A lopsided parent

Choose the exponential parent and set N = 1, so that the curve jumps to 1 at z = −1 and falls away to the right. Before setting N = 3, predict the shape of the curve.

5 · How fast is the approach?

Keep the exponential parent at N = 3, and recall that the uniform parent gave a largest gap of 0.024 at N = 3. Before setting N = 30, predict the largest gap at N = 30.

6 · What the theorem says

For any parent with a finite variance σ2, the standardised sum z = (UN − Nμ)/(σ√N) approaches the standard Gaussian as N grows, whatever the parent’s shape. Standardising fixes the mean at 0 and the variance at 1, so only the shape is left to change.

How fast it gets there depends on the parent. The symmetric uniform parent is within 0.014 of the Gaussian by N = 4; the skewed exponential parent is still 0.037 away at N = 30, because its skewness fades only as 1/√N. The marker on the plot shows where the largest gap sits.

The Physics

Adding Up Random Numbers · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

The sim adds N independent random numbers and plots the density of their sum, shifted and scaled, against the standard Gaussian bell. A marker shows where the two curves are furthest apart.

What you'll learn

  • What the mean and the spread of a sum of random numbers are.
  • How the density of a sum is built from the density of one term.
  • What shifting and scaling the sum does to it.
  • What the largest gap measures, and whether every parent distribution closes it at the same rate.
The plot as it opens: the uniform parent with N = 1. Solid: the exact density of z. Dashed: the standard Gaussian. The amber bar marks the largest gap.

What's on screen

  • Solid blue: the exact density of z, the sum of N draws shifted and scaled. It comes from convolving the parent with itself, with no random numbers drawn.
  • Dashed: the standard Gaussian density, the same curve at every N.
  • Amber bar: the largest gap, the place where |solid − dashed| is greatest. Its size is in the readouts.
See itLook at the opening arrangement. Watch for: the uniform parent with N = 1, and one solid curve and one dashed curve on the same axes.

03

One draw and its sum: mean and spread

Each draw xi comes from the same parent, with mean μ and variance σ2. The sim adds N of them, independently, to make UN = x1 + x2 + … + xN. The notes show that means add, and, for independent draws, that variances add too (equations 8.15 and 8.16), so:

Mean, variance and standard deviation of the sum of N independent draws.
ParentMean μVariance σ2σ
uniform, 0 to 11/21/120.289
exponential, e−x111

With N = 1 the sum is the parent itself. For the uniform parent, the density of z is then a flat box between z = −√3 = −1.73 and +1.73, of height 0.289. The standard Gaussian has a peak of 0.399 and runs on either side of the box, so the largest gap, 0.200, is at the edge of the box, where the box is 0.289 high and the Gaussian only 0.089.

The standard deviation of the sum, σ√N, grows more slowly than its mean, Nμ. This is the sentence in the notes just after equation 8.16, and it comes back below.

Key idea. The mean of a sum of N draws is Nμ and its standard deviation is σ√N.
See itChoose the exponential parent, with N = 1. Watch for: Nμ = 1.0 and σ√N = 1.000, the density jumping up at the left end of the curve, and a large gap.
04

Two draws: the sum is a triangle

To get a sum u from two draws, the first draw is x and the second must be u − x. Add up every way of doing this (a convolution):

For the uniform parent p = 1 between 0 and 1, and zero elsewhere. Problem 7 in the notes asks for this triangle.

The integral is the length of overlap of two unit intervals, as one slides over the other. A sum near 0 needs both draws near 0, and there is only one way to do it. A sum near 1 can be made in many ways, one small and one large. So the overlap rises in straight lines from 0 at u = 0 to its peak of 1 at u = 1, and falls back to 0 at u = 2. It is a triangle, with a sharp corner.

N = 2. Left: the density of U2. Right: the same sum in z, with the dashed Gaussian.

In z, with Nμ = 1.0 and σ√N = 0.408, the ends u = 0 and 2 become z = −√6 and +√6, which is ±2.45. The peak is 0.408, a little above the Gaussian's 0.399. The solid line stops at ±2.45, where the dashed curve goes on, and its shoulders lie above the dashed curve. The largest gap is 0.031, at about z = 1.66.

Key idea. The sum of two uniform draws is not uniform. Its density is a triangle, the overlap of two boxes.
See itChoose the uniform parent, with N = 1, then set N = 2. Watch for: the box turning into two sloping sides, with σ√N = 0.408.
05

Three draws and more: smoothing the corner

A third draw rounds the corner. At N = 3 the density is made of three pieces of parabola, and it is already a smooth bell. Its peak is 0.375, a little below the Gaussian's 0.399, and the largest gap, 0.024, sits at z = 0.

The uniform parent at N = 1, 2, 3 and 4. Solid: the density of z. Dashed: the standard Gaussian. Amber: the largest gap.

The largest gap falls with every extra draw. At N = 3 the notes say the density of the sum "is already close to a Gaussian". By N = 4 the solid curve is hard to tell from the dashed one. This is the uniform parent, which is symmetric about its mean. The next sections ask what happens when it is not.

Key idea. For the uniform parent, three or four draws already give a curve almost on top of the Gaussian.
See itKeep the uniform parent, and raise N from 2 to 3 and 4. Watch for: the curve rounding off, and the largest gap shrinking at each step.
06

Standardising: why the width stays put

UN itself does not stay still. The sim plots instead the sum shifted and scaled (the notes' equation 8.18), which has mean 0 and variance 1 for every N:

Standardised sum. Subtract the mean Nμ, divide by the standard deviation σ√N.

The uniform parent at N = 4 has Nμ = 2.0 and σ√N = 0.577. At N = 16 it has Nμ = 8.0 and σ√N = 1.155. The centre has moved four times as far, and the spread has doubled. The density of z follows from the rule for a change of variable (equation 8.17):

Uniform parent. Left: the density of UN for N = 4 and 16. Right: the density of z for the same two.

Dividing by σ√N takes away the growth in width, and subtracting Nμ takes away the drift. What is left is the shape. The curve to compare with is the standard Gaussian, which has mean 0 and variance 1:

The standard Gaussian density. Its peak is 1/√(2π) = 0.399, and it bends at z = ±1.
Key idea. In z the width is the same at every N. Only the shape changes, and the largest gap measures how much.
See itChoose the uniform parent with N = 4, then set N = 16. Watch for: Nμ going from 2.0 to 8.0 and σ√N from 0.577 to 1.155, while the solid curve is drawn at the same width as before.
07

A lopsided parent: a slower approach

The exponential parent is not symmetric. At N = 1 the density of z jumps to 1 at z = −1 and falls away to the right. The gap is 0.758 there, where the exponential reaches 1.00 and the Gaussian is 0.242.

The exponential parent at N = 1, 3 and 30.

At N = 3 the density of z is zero below z = −√3 and has a rounded peak of 0.469 at z = −1/√3 = −0.58, left of the Gaussian's peak, with a longer tail to the right. The largest gap is 0.161. At N = 30 the solid curve looks like a bell, but its peak, 0.405, is still left of z = 0, at z = −0.18, and the largest gap is 0.037.

NExponentialUniform
10.7580.200
30.1610.024
100.0700.006
300.0370.002

The table gives the largest gap for each parent. The theorem promises the limit, not the speed. The uniform parent is symmetric and has no lean to lose. The exponential has a lean, which fades only slowly: for a sum of N exponentials its skewness, a measure of the lean, is 2/√N. This last fact is outside the notes.

Key idea. Every parent with a finite variance approaches the Gaussian, but a lopsided parent needs far more terms than a symmetric one.
See itChoose the exponential parent, with N = 1, then set N = 3 and N = 30. Watch for: a peak that stays left of z = 0 even at N = 30, with the largest gap still far above the uniform parent’s.
08

Where it matters: sums of many small things

The central limit theorem says that for independent draws with the same distribution, with a mean and a finite variance, the standardised sum z approaches the standard Gaussian as N grows, whatever the distribution of the individual draws. The notes leave its proof beyond the course. Both parents in the sim have finite variance.

A binomial count is a sum of n independent draws, each 1 for a success and 0 for a failure. For large n it is close to a Gaussian. The error in a measurement is often a sum of many small independent disturbances, such as vibrations of the apparatus and variations in reaction time, and this is the usual reason for treating measurement errors as Gaussian.

The notes use it twice more. The chi-squared distribution is close to a Gaussian for many degrees of freedom, as for a sum of many terms. And the statistic (&xbar; − μ0)/(σ/√N), built from the mean of N values, is close to the standard Gaussian for large N (equation 8.35).

The sim computes the densities by repeated convolution, as the notes did for Figure 73. No random numbers are drawn, so what you see does not change from one run to the next.

09

Summary

In one line. The sim plots the density of a sum of N independent random numbers, shifted and scaled, against the standard Gaussian, and the largest gap measures how far apart they still are.

Common mix-ups

  • "Adding uniform numbers gives a uniform result." Two give a triangle, with a sharp corner.
  • "A sum of N numbers has a width that stays the same." UN has width σ√N. It is z, divided by this, that keeps the same width.
  • "All parents come as close as the uniform one." The uniform parent has a gap of 0.024 at N = 3. The exponential still has 0.037 at N = 30.
  • "At N = 30 the theorem has been reached." The theorem is a limit. The gap shrinks, and it is never exactly zero.

Things to try on your own

  • Uniform parent, N = 10. Nμ should read 5.0, σ√N 0.913 and the largest gap 0.006.
  • Exponential parent, N = 10. Nμ should read 10.0, σ√N 3.162 and the largest gap 0.070.
